data.cause: The primary-dns service on dns1.lan rate-limits the whole 10.20.0.0/24 client subnet to 20 queries/second and silently drops the excess, so during brief daily traffic spikes legitimate lookups of local names like nas.lan are dropped and clients see ENOTFOUND until the burst passes.
evidence: journalctl -u primary-dns on dns1.lan shows exactly the alert pattern: 'ratelimit: 10.20.0.0/24 exceeded 20 q/s, dropping 23 queries' at 02:14, 09:41-09:41:30 and 13:02, each immediately followed by 'back under limit' a second or two later — a few episodes per day, each self-clearing within about a minute.

cat /opt/primary-dns/config.yaml: ratelimit: 20 with ratelimit_subnet_len_ipv4: 24, i.e. one shared 20 q/s bucket for the entire /24 rather than per client; the .lan answers come only from this server's rewrites (domain '*.lan' -> 10.20.0.50).
dig @10.20.0.3 nas.lan on mon.lan normally succeeds (A 10.20.0.50) but with a TTL of only 10 seconds, so cached answers expire constantly and every lookup hits the rate-limited server again.

dig @10.20.0.1 nas.lan on mon.lan returns NOERROR with ANSWER: 0 — gw.lan's resolver has no local data of its own. cat /var/unbound/unbound.conf on gw.lan shows forward-zone name "lan." forward-addr 10.20.0.3 with forward-first: yes, so the backup resolver depends on the very server that is dropping queries; internet names instead go via forward-addr 1.1.1.2@853 / 9.9.9.9@853, which is why public names are unaffected.
data.recommendation: Raise or disable the ratelimit on dns1.lan's primary-dns service (config.yaml: ratelimit: 20 is far too low for a shared /24; use per-client accounting, e.g. ratelimit_subnet_len_ipv4: 32, and/or a much higher bucket), then reload the service. Optionally also raise the TTL on the .lan rewrite records so brief drops don't reach clients, and consider having gw.lan serve authoritative .lan data instead of forwarding to dns1 so one saturated server can't take out both configured resolvers.
